name: fastjson (valyala)
workload: Parse/validate six standard JSON corpora (small 190B, medium 2.3KB, large 28KB, canada 2.2MB, citm_catalog 1.7MB, twitter 617KB) single-threaded (GOMAXPROCS=1) with Go's testing/benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: README: 'up to 15x faster than encoding/json'; benchmark table shows e.g. citm_catalog parse 918.87 MB/s (fastjson) vs 62.19 MB/s (stdjson-map) ~14.8x, canada 538.22 MB/s vs 33.03 MB/s ~16.3x, twitter 815.86 MB/s vs 55.94 MB/s ~14.6x; JSON validation 1025 MB/s vs 237 MB/s (~4.3x) on citm_catalog
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.12, `go test -bench` (GOMAXPROCS=1); no later Go version re-run published
tradeoffs: Zero-copy/zero-allocation parser but not a drop-in replacement API; caller must respect object-lifetime rules (Parser/Arena reuse) or risk misuse; validates JSON (unlike jsonparser/gjson) at some cost vs those libraries; can't parse from io.Reader directly.
caveats: Benchmark numbers are from a 2019-era README run on Go 1.12; no CPU model stated and not re-run against modern Go versions/encoding/json (which itself has improved since); first-party benchmark only.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fast json parser" --sort stars

name: sonic-rs
workload: Deserialize/serialize standard corpora (twitter.json, citm_catalog.json, canada.json) into typed Rust structs and into an untyped Value/DOM, via Criterion (`cargo bench`).
claimed_speedup: canada untyped deserialize: 4.91-4.98ms (sonic_rs) vs 16.98-16.64ms (serde_json) ~3.4x, vs 12.03-12.85ms (simd-json Rust) ~2.5x; twitter struct deserialize: 695-723us (unchecked) vs 2266-2317us (serde_json::from_slice) ~3.2x, vs 1062-1115us (simd-json) ~1.5x; twitter serialize: 381-400us (sonic_rs) vs 789-808us (serde_json) ~2x, vs 966-998us (simd-json) ~2.4x
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench (Criterion); rustflags `-C target-cpu=native` required for SIMD codegen (exact rustc version not stated)
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8260 CPU @ 2.40GHz (x86_64); AArch64 numbers reported separately in docs/benchmark_aarch64.md
tradeoffs: Fastest on x86_64/aarch64 only, falls back (slow) on other architectures; requires `-C target-cpu=native` for full speed which hurts binary portability; `sanitize` feature causes ~30% perf loss under LLVM sanitizers.
caveats: Numbers are from the project's own README/benchmark suite (not an independent third party), though the benchmark code, CPU model, and dataset are all public and reproducible; rustc/cargo version used for the numbers is not pinned in the README.

name: reflect-cpp
workload: Read/write three datasets (canada - float-heavy, licenses - nested/string-heavy, person - small) using C++20 reflection-based (de)serialization vs. hand-written RapidJSON/nlohmann::json code, run via Google Benchmark in CI.
claimed_speedup: Benchmarks README: 'reflect-cpp is consistently faster than RapidJSON, usually about twice as fast' and 'consistently about 10 times faster than nlohmann/json'; also states reflect-cpp is 'slightly slower than the fastest JSON libraries for C and C++, namely simdJSON and yyjson' because its JSON backend is built on yyjson
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.4 on Ubuntu 22.04, CMake Release build (-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release), Google Benchmark harness; also run continuously in GitHub Actions across compilers/OSes/architectures
tradeoffs: reflect-cpp's JSON path is a thin reflection layer over yyjson, so its speed advantage is really 'yyjson plus near-zero-overhead reflection' vs hand-written RapidJSON/nlohmann code; requires C++20 reflection features; exact numeric results are only published as chart images in CI artifacts, not as text tables in the repo.
caveats: Result values (the actual read/write times) are shown only as PNG charts in benchmarks/img/, not as numbers in the README text; no CPU model is given, only 'gcc 11.4 on Ubuntu 22.4'; comparison is first-party (reflect-cpp's own repo).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "boost.json" --sort stars (reflect-cpp appeared in results; description mentions Boost Serialization/JSON support)

name: jsoncons
workload: Read and write two large synthetic JSON files (540.82MB text+integers, 794.72MB text+floating point) into each library's native document type, on a Windows workstation.
claimed_speedup: Integer file: jsoncons reads in 3.918s / writes in 0.744s vs nlohmann 8.177s / 2.885s (~2.1x read, ~3.9x write faster than nlohmann); vs RapidJSON 2.254s / 0.656s, jsoncons is slower on read, slower on write (derived from page data). Float file: jsoncons 8.879s / 3.879s vs nlohmann 15.997s / 7.165s (~1.8x faster both ways); vs RapidJSON 3.443s / 3.061s, jsoncons is slower (derived from page data)
hardware: Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Extreme, 8 cores / 16 hardware threads, 32GB RAM, 2TB SSD, Windows (exact CPU model name not given, only laptop model/core count)
tradeoffs: jsoncons beats nlohmann/json clearly but is not the fastest option in this same shootout (yyjson and RapidJSON both beat it on these workloads); jsoncons trades some speed for API breadth (JSON Pointer/Patch/Path, JMESPath, multiple binary formats).
caveats: This is a shootout run by the jsoncons author comparing many libraries (not an independent lab), single machine/single run reported, and library versions are pinned to whatever was current when the report was generated; exact CPU model is not named, only laptop model and core/thread count.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "jsoncons" --sort stars, then gh api repos/danielaparker/json_benchmarks/contents/report/*.md

name: Boost.JSON
workload: Same shootout as jsoncons entry: read/write two large synthetic JSON files (540.82MB integers, 794.72MB floats) into boost::json::value, on a Windows workstation.
claimed_speedup: Integer file: Boost.JSON reads in 2.269s / writes in 0.585s vs nlohmann 8.177s / 2.885s (~3.6x read, ~4.9x write faster); vs RapidJSON 2.254s / 0.656s, Boost.JSON is essentially tied on read and ~1.1x faster on write (derived from page data). Float file: Boost.JSON 3.579s / 2.722s vs nlohmann 15.997s / 7.165s (~4.5x read, ~2.6x write faster); vs RapidJSON 3.443s / 3.061s, Boost.JSON is slightly slower on read but ~1.1x faster on write (derived from page data)
hardware: Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Extreme, 8 cores / 16 hardware threads, 32GB RAM, 2TB SSD, Windows (exact CPU model name not given)
stars_or_usage: 479 stars on the standalone mirror (Boost.JSON ships as part of the wider Boost distribution, so GitHub stars understate real usage)
tradeoffs: Requires (or vendors) the wider Boost dependency footprint even though Boost.JSON itself is usable header-only/standalone; API is more verbose than nlohmann's for simple use cases; memory footprint (502MB/621MB in this test) sits between RapidJSON and yyjson.
caveats: Same third-party shootout caveats as the jsoncons entry: single machine/run, no exact CPU model, benchmark maintained by a competing library's author (danielaparker/jsoncons) rather than the Boost project itself.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "boost.json" --sort stars, then gh api repos/danielaparker/json_benchmarks/contents/report/*.md

name: segmentio/encoding (encoding/json replacement)
workload: Marshal/Unmarshal a large nested Go struct (`*json.codeResponse2`, the standard Go JSON benchmark corpus) via CI-run Go benchmarks, compared against the stdlib and against json-iterator/go.
claimed_speedup: Marshal 6.40ms -> 3.82ms (-40.3%, ~1.68x), Unmarshal 28.1ms -> 5.6ms (-80.2%, ~5.02x) vs encoding/json v1.16.2; throughput 303MB/s->507MB/s marshal (+67%), 69.2MB/s->349.6MB/s unmarshal (+405%); allocations cut from 1.80MB/76.6k allocs to 0.02MB/0.1k allocs per unmarshal op. Also ~1.53x faster marshal and ~1.53x faster unmarshal than json-iterator/go v1.1.10
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain (exact version not stated in README); benchmarks run via CI on every change
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; used in production at Segment/Twilio
tradeoffs: Drop-in API-compatible replacement for encoding/json (just change the import path), but relies heavily on unsafe pointer arithmetic instead of reflect, and does not (yet) support streaming decode of JSON arrays the way the stdlib Decoder does.
caveats: Numbers are from the project's own CI benchmark comparison, single CPU model, exact Go version not pinned in the README; only one benchmark case (codeResponse2) is shown in the top-level README even though more exist in the repo.
found_via: Direct lookup of a well-known Go encoding/json replacement, verified via gh api repos/segmentio/encoding and its README this session

name: simdjson-go
workload: Unmarshal-to-interface{} across 14 real-world JSON test files (apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc_2018, instruments, marine_ik, mesh, mesh_pretty, numbers, random, twitter, twitterescaped, update_center) using `benchcmp`, GOMAXPROCS=32.
claimed_speedup: README: 'compared to Golang's standard package encoding/json, simdjson-go is about 10x faster' (and 'runs on average at about 40% to 60% of the speed of simdjson' C++). Per-file speedups range 2.34x (Numbers) to 16.50x (Gsoc_2018), e.g. Twitter 95.17->1072.59 MB/s (11.27x), Citm_catalog 101.29->1270.02 MB/s (12.54x)
compiler_and_flags: Go, `go test -bench` with `benchcmp` (compiler version and build flags not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires AVX2 + CLMUL CPU support with no software fallback (fails closed rather than degrading); pure Go (no cgo) but effectively a from-scratch reimplementation of simdjson's two-stage algorithm, not a wrapper around the C++ library, so it inherits simdjson's tape-based access model rather than idiomatic Go structs.
caveats: No CPU model is stated for the benchmark numbers, only GOMAXPROCS=32; repo has had no commits in about 13 months as of this run (stale by this pipeline's definition), though it is still depended on by MinIO in production.
found_via: Direct lookup of the known Go port of simdjson, verified via gh api repos/minio/simdjson-go and its README this session

name: orjson
workload: Serialize/deserialize twitter.json, github.json, citm_catalog.json, and canada.json using orjson vs. the CPython standard library `json` module, via the `pybench` reproduction script.
claimed_speedup: Median latency vs. stdlib json: twitter.json serialize 0.1ms vs 1.3ms (11.1x), deserialize 0.5ms vs 2.2ms (4.2x); github.json serialize 0.01ms vs 0.13ms (13.6x), deserialize 0.04ms vs 0.1ms (2.2x); citm_catalog.json serialize 0.3ms vs 3ms (11.8x), deserialize 1.3ms vs 4ms (3.1x); canada.json serialize 2.5ms vs 29.8ms (11.9x), deserialize 3ms vs 18ms (6x)
compiler_and_flags: Rust (packaged with maturin, `maturin build --release --strip`); measured using CPython 3.11.10, wheel `orjson-3.10.11-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux2014_x86_64.whl`
hardware: x86-64-v4 machine, Fedora 42 container (exact CPU model not named)
stars_or_usage: 8.2k stars; widely used in the Python ecosystem (FastAPI, Django integrations, etc.)
tradeoffs: Only usable from Python (Rust internals are not exposed as a Rust crate); does not serialize to str (bytes-only) or support object_hook/NDJSON; also independently verified against `nativejson-benchmark`'s conformance corpus (0 invalid-docs-accepted / 0 valid-docs-rejected vs 17/0 for stdlib json).
caveats: Baseline is Python's stdlib json module, not one of RapidJSON/nlohmann/simdjson/serde_json, so baseline_in_list=false; numbers are first-party (orjson's own README), reproducible via a published script, but the exact CPU model is not named, only the microarchitecture level (x86-64-v4).

name: Mison (speculative structural-index JSON parser)
workload: Single-threaded field-projection queries (Q1-Q8) over real-world Twitter (25-38 fields/record), Yelp, and GitHub JSON datasets, comparing parsing throughput (GB/s) of Mison vs Gson, Jackson, and RapidJSON using each library's streaming-mode API.
claimed_speedup: Paper (Fig. 8, Sec 6.1.1): 'Mison is between 5.5 and 9.1 times faster than the best competitor' on Twitter Q1-Q8, with the best case (8-9x) on simple queries over mandatory fields; Sec 6.1.2/Fig.10: on the GitHub dataset without projection push-down, Mison still 'outperforms the best existing JSON parser (Jackson) by a factor of 2'; Fig.11: basic (non-speculative) Mison already beats Jackson by 3.6x, full speculative Mison by 10.2x on Twitter
compiler_and_flags: Implemented as a C++ static library; structural-index construction uses AVX2 (256-bit SIMD); exact compiler/version not stated in the paper
hardware: 3.5GHz Intel Xeon Broadwell-EP E5-1620 v3, 16GB DDR3 RAM, 64-bit Windows 10, single-threaded runs
stars_or_usage: Published VLDB 2017 (PVLDB Vol. 10, No. 10, pp. 1118-1129) by Microsoft Research and University of Pittsburgh; no official source release found
tradeoffs: Requires an offline training phase to build 'pattern trees' from sample data before speculative parsing works well; benefit shrinks as the fraction of queried fields grows (Fig. 12) and for highly irregular/schema-varying JSON; only helps analytical/partial-field workloads, not full-document parse+build (Sec 6.1, 'if all fields are needed... [binary formats are] still the most efficient approach').
caveats: No public source code was found for Mison itself (only unofficial, low-star third-party reimplementations exist, e.g. ubnt-intrepid/misosoup, indiependente/gomison, neither independently benchmarked); per this run's rules, a paper with no code is capped at tier C despite being peer-reviewed with full hardware/methodology disclosure; hardware is now an old (2015-era) CPU.
found_via: WebSearch: "Mison A Fast JSON Parser for Data Analytics VLDB rapidjson speedup pdf"; paper opened directly at vldb.org

name: ssrJSON
workload: dumps/loads across twitter.json, github.json, citm_catalog.json, canada.json (floats), mesh.json (numbers), and simple_object_zh.json (non-ASCII text), using the companion `ssrjson-benchmark` package, on Python 3.14 with AVX2.
claimed_speedup: README: 'ssrjson.dumps() is about 4x-31x as fast as json.dumps()' and 'ssrjson.loads() is about 2x-8x as fast as json.loads()' for both str and bytes input (Python 3.14, x86-64, AVX2); also claims to be 'faster than or nearly as fast as orjson... on most benchmark cases' per its ratio-distribution chart
compiler_and_flags: Must be built with Clang (uses Clang vector extensions; cannot build with GCC or pure MSVC, clang-cl on Windows); CMake Release build
hardware: x86-64 with AVX2 (exact CPU model not stated for the main dumps/loads benchmark; a separate float-formatting micro-benchmark states 'Apple M1' and 'AMD R7-7840H')
tradeoffs: Beta-quality, several standard json-module features not yet implemented; requires Clang specifically to build; only supports x86-64-v2+ (SSE4.2 minimum) and aarch64, no 32-bit or older-CPU fallback; enabling its UTF-8 str cache trades memory for speed on repeated encodes.
caveats: Very new/low-star project (39 stars); its headline numbers are shown only as SVG charts, not text tables, and the exact CPU model for the primary dumps/loads benchmark is not stated; baseline is Python's stdlib json, not one of this run's named baselines, so baseline_in_list=false; author is also the source of the 'faster than orjson' claim (first-party).
found_via: HN Algolia: query="faster json parser simd", tags=story (surfaced 'Show HN: SsrJSON: faster than the fastest Python JSON library')
